problem: End-to-end learned visuomotor controllers (e.g., the NVIDIA self-driving net) map perception directly to control. They cannot be steered toward arbitrary goals: at an intersection the right action depends on the goal, so plain imitation averages conflicting expert behavior. Classical map-based navigation instead needs accurate SLAM maps and fails on things like glass doors, people and unmapped obstacles.
motivation: Humans reach any location in a new building from only an abstract 2-D floor plan. They do it by combining coarse global planning with robust local visual execution. The authors want a delivery robot to do the same in a new office building with minimal prior information (a digitized visitor floor plan), by pairing model-based planning with model-free deep learning.
key_idea: A two-level hierarchy: a hybrid-A* planner on a crude floor-plan occupancy grid replans every step and emits an 'intention'. The intention is either a discrete local move or a local path-and-environment image. It conditions an imitation-learned CNN controller (intention-net) that maps a monocular image plus the intention to speed and steering.
insight: Conditioning the learned controller on the planner's intention is what makes it goal-directed and generalizable. The ablation without intention and without planner ('Non-Intention Net') succeeds only on Task A, which has no junctions, and fails Tasks B–E because it blindly mimics experts who had different goals. The planner-only 'Path Tracker' with no visual feedback completes all tasks but needs up to 21 human interventions (Task E) and moves jerkily. The richer LPE intention (local map + path image) beats the 4-value DLM, especially in unseen environments (Tasks D/E) and on sharp turns in the real robot. The dominant real-world failure is a wrong intention caused by localization error, which points to localization as the bottleneck.
method: High-level planner: crude 2-D floor plan converted to an occupancy grid; AMCL localizes the robot (LIDAR); hybrid A* replans a path from the current pose to the goal at every time step.
DLM intention: the local signed curvature of the planned path is thresholded into TurnLeft/TurnRight/GoForward, with Stop at the goal.
LPE intention: a 224×224 image of the local map window showing the traversed path (red), the path ahead (blue) and the robot position.

DLM-Net: ResNet50 (no final FC) extracts a 2048-d image feature; the one-hot intention (4) is expanded to 64-d and concatenated; an FC layer outputs controls for all intentions, and the input intention selects which one is used.

LPE-Net: a two-stream siamese ResNet50 with shared weights processes the camera image and the intention image; the two 2048-d features are concatenated and an FC layer regresses the control (speed v, steering θ).

Imitation learning: (image, intention, control) tuples come from a DWA expert in simulation and a human joystick expert on the real robot. Outputs are normalized to [-1,1]. Training uses RMSprop (lr 1e-4, L2 1e-4, lr/(1+k) decay), batch size 8, and 200,000 resampled samples per epoch from a dataset pool.

setting.backbone: ResNet50 feature extractor + FC regression head (DLM-Net / siamese LPE-Net), trained via imitation learning; hybrid A* planner (non-learned) at the high level
setting.training_data: Demonstrations: in simulation, a dynamic-window-approach expert on hand-sketched Stage maps; on the real robot, human joystick demonstrations on the first floor of an office building. 4:1 train/eval split; 200k resampled samples per epoch. Dataset size not stated.
setting.observation: monocular RGB camera image (224×224; 70° FOV webcam on the real robot) + planner-derived intention (discrete move or local map/path image); LIDAR used only for AMCL localization
setting.privileged: crude 2-D floor-plan map (digitized visitor floor plan) given; robot pose from LIDAR-based AMCL on that map; goal location given

numbers_note: Table 1 row labels are LaTeX macros. They were mapped from context: \IN = DLM-Net, \IMN = LPE-Net, \BLIND = Path Tracker, \PURE = Non-Intention Net, \DWA = Dynamic Window. Success is reported only as Y/N and Smoothness is average jerk (lower is better). Each task is a single run through a sequence of goals; there are no aggregate SR statistics. Real-robot results are qualitative only (moving people, glass doors, generalization to the second floor), with no quantitative numbers.
results: In five Stage-simulated tasks, DLM-Net and LPE-Net both complete every task with zero human interventions. The ablations fall short: Non-Intention Net fails Tasks B–E, and Path Tracker needs 3/16/5/21 interventions on B–E and moves jerkily. Both intention-nets also beat the Dynamic Window baseline on time and smoothness in the more complex tasks; for example, on the Task E maze LPE-Net takes 531 s with smoothness 0.0075 versus DWA's 551 s and 0.0084. On a Pioneer 3-DX with a webcam, the intention-net qualitatively handles moving people and an unseen glass door, and transfers from the first to the second office floor.
limitations: Localization is a black box (LIDAR AMCL on a crude map). Localization errors produce wrong intentions, which is the most common failure (e.g., GoForward instead of TurnLeft at a hallway end).
The evaluation is preliminary: one run per task on 5 hand-sketched Stage tasks, and the real-robot results are qualitative only with no quantitative success rates.
The DLM intention is limited to 4 discrete values with a hand-set curvature threshold, which is inadequate for junctions with more branches.
